title: Chest trauma
subtitle: The six that kill early

sources.org: American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma
sources.title: Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) Student Course Manual
NEXUS Chest decision instruments for blunt chest trauma imaging

red_flags.text: Tension pneumothorax: respiratory distress, absent breath sounds, hyperresonance, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation late.
Open pneumothorax: a sucking chest wound larger than about two-thirds of the tracheal diameter.
Massive haemothorax: a silent, dull hemithorax with shock.
Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds; often only hypotension in a hypovolaemic patient.
Flail segment with paradoxical movement and rising oxygen requirement.
Tracheobronchial injury: massive air leak, persistent pneumothorax after a well-placed drain, surgical emphysema.

do_now.text: Decompress a tension pneumothorax immediately on clinical grounds. Finger or needle thoracostomy first, formal drain after.
Cover an open chest wound with a dressing sealed on three sides, then place a chest drain away from the wound.
High-flow oxygen, analgesia adequate enough to allow deep breathing, and continuous monitoring.
Suspected tamponade in a peri-arrest patient goes to theatre or resuscitative thoracotomy, not to the CT scanner.

assess.text: Expose the whole chest, front and back. Count respiratory rate yourself; it is the earliest sign and the least recorded.
Percuss and auscultate both sides at matched levels, then palpate for crepitus, flail and tenderness.
Distended neck veins with shock narrow the diagnosis to tension pneumothorax, tamponade or cardiac contusion.
Track drain output and air leak continuously once a drain is in. The trend is the decision.
Apply a validated rule before imaging a stable blunt-trauma patient rather than scanning reflexively.

investigate.text: Supine chest radiograph in the resuscitation room. It is a screening film, not an exclusion test.
eFAST for pericardial fluid, pneumothorax and haemothorax at the bedside.
CT with contrast for the stabilised patient: it finds the aortic injury, the diaphragmatic tear and the occult pneumothorax.
ECG and troponin for suspected blunt cardiac injury; a normal ECG in a haemodynamically normal patient largely excludes it.
Arterial gas for oxygenation and ventilation trend in a flail chest or pulmonary contusion.

resuscitate.text: Aggressive multimodal analgesia including regional block for rib fractures. Pain control is the treatment that prevents pneumonia.
Blood rather than crystalloid for a haemothorax with shock; the chest drain output is external blood loss.
Chest physiotherapy, sitting up and early mobilisation from day one in blunt chest wall injury.
Non-invasive ventilation or intubation for a failing flail chest, guided by work of breathing and gas trend rather than a single saturation.

definitive.text: Chest drain for pneumothorax and haemothorax. Most chest trauma is treated with a drain and good analgesia.
Thoracotomy for an immediate drain output above roughly 1500 mL, or a continuing loss of about 200 mL per hour for several hours, or for a patient who will not stabilise.
Surgical rib fixation is considered in selected flail chest and severely displaced fractures; it is a planned decision, not an emergency one.
Persistent large air leak or failure of the lung to re-expand needs bronchoscopy and a thoracic surgical opinion.

escalate.text: Cardiothoracic or major-trauma centre for suspected aortic injury, tracheobronchial injury, or penetrating mediastinal trauma.
Critical care for flail chest, significant contusion, or an oxygen requirement that is climbing.
Anyone with three or more rib fractures, or any rib fracture in an elderly patient, needs a higher level of observation than they look like they need.

notes: Most chest trauma is managed with oxygen, analgesia and a drain. The skill is spotting the minority who need more, early.
Elderly patients with a small number of rib fractures have a mortality that is consistently underestimated at the front door.
